title: Implement a natural resource management plan

lessons.title: Understanding the natural resource management plan
lessons.html:
What the plan contains

A natural resource management (NRM) plan sets out how a farm will protect and improve its soil, water, vegetation and biodiversity while producing profitably. It is usually developed by the farm manager with advisers such as extension officers, soil scientists, veld specialists or conservation bodies. At NQF level 4 you are responsible for turning the plan into action in the field.

Typical components

  • Resource inventory and maps: soils, land capability, slopes, water sources, wetlands, rivers, veld types, alien plant infestations, erosion sites, sensitive and protected areas.
  • Objectives and targets: for example, reduce bare soil in lands below a set percentage, clear a set area of wattle per year, restore a donga, rest each grazing camp for a full growing season in rotation.
  • Soil conservation measures: contour banks, waterways, conservation agriculture practices, gully rehabilitation.
  • Water management: irrigation scheduling, water use within registered or licensed entitlements, buffer zones along rivers and wetlands, pollution prevention.
  • Veld and grazing management: carrying capacity, stocking rate, rotation and rest, fire regime, bush encroachment control.
  • Alien and invasive plant control: priority areas and methods.
  • Biodiversity: conservation of indigenous vegetation, corridors and species of concern.
  • Waste and pollution control.
  • Monitoring and reporting.

Legal framework

The Conservation of Agricultural Resources Act 43 of 1983 sets duties for land users on soil, water, vegetation and weeds and invader plants. The National Water Act 36 of 1998 governs water use and protection of water resources. Other environmental legislation applies to activities such as clearing indigenous vegetation or developing in wetlands; check with the relevant authority before such work.

From plan to action

Break the plan into an annual work programme: specific tasks, locations, timing, responsibilities, resources and budget.

lessons.title: Implementing, monitoring and reporting
lessons.html:
Organising implementation

  1. Prioritise tasks by risk and urgency, such as repairing a breached contour bank before the rains, or clearing aliens before they seed.
  2. Schedule work around production peaks and seasons: alien follow-up clearing in the growing season, earthworks in the dry season, burning only in the prescribed window with the required permits and fire protection association rules.
  3. Allocate teams, equipment, materials and budget.
  4. Brief and train teams on methods and safety.

Implementation examples

ActivityImplementation points
Alien clearingCut, then treat stumps with a registered herbicide per label where required; follow-up clearing of seedlings; stack or remove biomass safely
Gully rehabilitationDivert water above the head, build stone or brush check structures, reshape and revegetate
Grazing rotationMove animals per grazing chart, monitor grass height and condition, adjust for rainfall
Riparian buffersFence off where planned, provide alternative water points, remove aliens, allow indigenous regrowth
Conservation agricultureRetain residues, use no-till planters, plan rotations and cover crops

Safety

Chainsaws and brush cutters need trained operators with full PPE. Herbicide use requires trained applicators, label PPE and care near water. Controlled burns need firebreaks, sufficient crew and equipment, suitable weather and compliance with fire laws.

Monitoring

  • Fixed-point photographs before and after work
  • Area cleared, banks repaired, metres fenced
  • Veld condition, grass cover and stocking records
  • Water use and quality records
  • Costs per activity

Reporting and adaptive management

Report progress against targets to management regularly. When results fall short, investigate why, such as poor follow-up, drought or budget limits, and adjust methods or timing. NRM is long term: consistent follow-through matters more than one-off projects.

Stakeholders

Work with neighbours, conservancies, fire protection associations, water user associations and government programmes for alien clearing and land care.

Key points

  • The NRM plan covers soil, water, veld, aliens, biodiversity and pollution.
  • Translate the plan into a prioritised annual work programme.
  • Time work to seasons and follow legal requirements.
  • Use trained operators and PPE for chainsaws, herbicides and fire.
  • Monitor, report and adapt the plan over time.
